sources.title: Sable Antelope
sources.note: 2025 regional assessment: Vulnerable; regional trend stable. Kruger subpopulation described as increasing.

size.note: Head-and-body length 190–255 cm and tail 40–75 cm follow Wikipedia. Shoulder height: Wikipedia gives males at about 117–140 cm, females slightly shorter; Animal Diversity Web gives 116–142 cm for males. The overall bounds used here are 116–142 cm. Mass was published only as typical values (Wikipedia: males 235 kg, females 220 kg; ADW: males around 238 kg, females 220 kg), not as ranges, so massKg is left null. Horns are 81–165 cm in males and 61–102 cm in females.

summary: A large, dark antelope of wooded savanna, with a white belly, a strongly marked black-and-white face, and long, backswept scimitar horns in both sexes. Adult males are almost black; females and young are rich brown. It is one of Kruger's scarce, slowly recovering antelope. The official English name on the 2011 checklist is Sable.
description: Adult males are glossy black or very dark brown, with a white belly, white face markings that contrast with a dark mask, and a mane on the neck. Females are chestnut to dark brown, also with a white belly and a pale face pattern, and are slightly smaller. Both sexes have ringed, scimitar-shaped horns that arch backward, longer and more curved in males (81–165 cm) than in females (61–102 cm). Newborn calves are sandy or light tan, which helps to camouflage them, and the coat darkens with age. The official checklist name is Sable; iNaturalist prefers Sable Antelope. The critically endangered giant sable of Angola is a different subspecies and is not the Kruger animal.
habits: Lives in herds of about 10 to 30 females and calves, led by a single bull. Males fight on their knees with their horns. When threatened, sable may stand and fight rather than flee, and can injure a predator with the backswept horns. They are mainly diurnal, but less active in the heat of the day. In Kruger the species is scarce and is described as slowly increasing after a sharp decline.

diet.summary: A grazer of mid-length grasses that also takes leaves and herbs. Animal Diversity Web describes feeding on grasses 40–140 mm high. It visits salt licks and has been recorded chewing bones for minerals.

young: A single calf is born after a gestation of about nine months, with births coinciding with the rainy season in the general account. The newborn is sandy or light tan and lies hidden for at least ten days while the mother nurses it. The coat darkens as the animal grows. Exact calving months for Kruger were not found.

predators.note: Not a mammal in this guide; listed because it is a documented predator of this species.

habitat: Wooded savanna and grassland, including the mixed bush of Kruger. Photographs in this file come from the Lower Sabie, Tshokwane and Pretoriuskop areas as well as other parts of the park.

similar.note: Sable is darker, with a white belly, a strongly contrasted black-and-white face, and longer, more arched scimitar horns. Roan is paler (roan or grey-brown) and heavier, with shorter, less backswept horns and a different face pattern.

population.notes: One source claims a 2023 Kruger population of 384–470 sable, and describes the species as rare and slowly increasing, one of four antelope that crashed in the 1990s. The EWT 2025 assessment gives a current Kruger estimate of 256–299 mature individuals and describes the Kruger subpopulation as increasing. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf Regional Red List status is Vulnerable, with a stable national trend.
